Initially, Professor B noted that training on one language and testing on another resulted in poor performance. However, they questioned whether broad training data across multiple languages could improve performance when tested on a different language. Professor B observed that adding more training data did not necessarily improve performance on specific tasks like TI-digits. They concluded that the presence of a particular language in the training set did not significantly affect performance, suggesting that the difference in performance between including or excluding a language was minimal. PhD D provided additional insights, noting that training on Spanish and testing on Italian showed a notably higher error rate compared to the baseline, indicating that the closeness of languages might influence performance.
